title: What an operating system is
subtitle: One program that manages every other: it shares the hardware, hides its ugliness, and draws the line between trusted and untrusted code. This chapter builds the whole picture before the later chapters take it apart.

why.title: The bare machine, and why nobody wants it
why.body:
Imagine you are handed a computer with nothing installed on it. There is a processor that executes instructions, some memory that holds bytes, a disk that stores blocks of 512 or 4096 bytes, a network card that sends frames, a keyboard that raises a signal when a key goes down. That is all the hardware offers. To print the word “hello” you would have to know which register of which controller chip to write, in what order, with what timing, and then wait politely for the device to say it is done. To store a file you would decide which sectors it occupies and remember that decision yourself. To run two programs you would have to make sure neither overwrites the other’s memory. Early programmers did exactly this, by hand, one program at a time.

An operating system (OS) exists to end that misery. It is a program — the first one to run and the last one to stop — whose job is to stand between every other program and the hardware. Nobody sets out to use an operating system; people use a browser, a compiler, a game. The OS is the thing that makes those programs possible to write at all, because it supplies the vocabulary they speak: files, processes, windows, sockets. When an application asks for “the file called report.txt” it is not asking the disk anything; it is asking the OS, which knows how to turn that sentence into sector numbers.

It helps to keep two descriptions of the OS in your head at once, because every design question in this subject is a tension between them. Seen from above — from the application programmer’s chair — the OS is an extended machine: a cleaner, friendlier, more powerful computer than the real one. Seen from below — from the hardware’s chair — the OS is a resource manager: a referee that hands out the processor, memory and devices to competing programs and makes sure they behave. The first description explains abstractions; the second explains policies. Most of this book is one or the other.

extended.title: The OS as an extended machine
extended.body:
Each abstraction the OS offers replaces something ugly with something usable. A file replaces numbered disk blocks: you read bytes at an offset, not sectors on a cylinder. A process replaces “the CPU”: each program believes it has a processor to itself, though the hardware has far fewer processors than programs. An address space replaces physical memory: every process sees a private, contiguous array of bytes starting at zero. A socket replaces a network card: two programs exchange a byte stream without thinking about frames, retransmissions or routes. A window replaces a rectangle of pixels in the frame buffer.

Notice what these abstractions have in common. They are all lies that are useful. The disk is not a tree of folders, the memory is not private, and the CPU is not yours — but behaving as if they were makes programs short, portable and safe. A good abstraction hides exactly the detail that varies between machines. That is why the same C program that calls read() works on an SSD, a spinning disk, a USB stick or a network file system: the abstraction is the same, and the OS (through its drivers) does the translation underneath.

The figure follows one tiny request, read(fd, buffer, 4096), downwards through the layers and back up. Watch how many different pieces of the system each take a turn: the system-call boundary, the file system that maps the file offset to a block, the buffer cache that might already hold it, the driver, the controller, and the physical disk. The application sees none of this; it sees only that the buffer is full when read returns.

manager.title: The OS as a resource manager
manager.body:
Now look from below. A computer has a handful of expensive, shareable resources: processor time, memory space, disk space, device access, network bandwidth. Several programs, and often several people, want them at once. Someone has to decide who gets what, and when. That someone is the OS, and its job has three parts that always travel together: allocation (hand out the resource), protection (stop one user from damaging another), and accounting (keep track of who used how much, for fairness or billing).

Resources are shared in one of two ways. Some are shared in time — the CPU and the printer are used by one program at a time, taking turns, so the OS’s job is to decide the order and the length of each turn (scheduling). Others are shared in space — memory and disk are divided into pieces and each program gets its own piece at the same moment, so the OS’s job is to carve, track and reclaim the pieces (memory management, file allocation). Almost every OS algorithm you will meet is either a time-sharing policy or a space-sharing policy.

Keep one more idea in mind: mechanism versus policy. A mechanism is how something is done (a timer interrupt that stops a running program every 10 ms); a policy is what is decided (which program runs next). Good systems keep the two separate so the policy can change without rewriting the machinery. When the exam asks you to “compare scheduling algorithms”, you are comparing policies that all run on the same mechanism.

hardware.title: What the hardware must provide: modes, interrupts, protection
hardware.body:
An operating system cannot enforce anything unless the hardware helps. If every instruction could be executed by every program, any program could disable interrupts, overwrite the OS or read your files. So processors provide a small set of features that make an OS possible. The first is the dual mode of operation: a mode bit that is either user or kernel (supervisor). In user mode the CPU refuses privileged instructions — I/O, changing the memory map, halting the machine, disabling interrupts. In kernel mode everything is allowed. Applications run in user mode; only the kernel runs in kernel mode, and the only way into kernel mode is through a controlled entry point (a system call, an interrupt, or a trap).

The second feature is memory protection: base and limit registers (or, in modern CPUs, page tables managed by a memory-management unit) that make each process’s addresses legal only inside its own region. A wild pointer then causes a fault the kernel can handle, instead of silently corrupting a neighbour. The third is the timer: a device that interrupts the CPU after a set interval, guaranteeing the OS regains control even from a program stuck in an infinite loop. Without the timer, a single buggy program could keep the processor forever; with it, preemptive multitasking is possible.

The fourth feature, and the one that makes I/O efficient, is the interrupt: a signal from a device (or from the CPU itself) that makes the processor stop what it is doing, save its place, run a handler and then resume. Instead of the CPU asking the disk every microsecond “are you finished yet?” (polling), the disk taps the CPU on the shoulder when it is. The next sections show the two ways to cross from user into kernel mode: voluntarily (a system call) and involuntarily (an interrupt or exception).

syscall.title: System calls: the controlled doorway
syscall.body:
A system call is a request from a user program for a service only the kernel may perform. In C you rarely see one directly; you call a library function such as printf, fopen or malloc, and the library, at the right moment, executes a special instruction (syscall, int 0x80, svc) that traps into the kernel. The CPU switches to kernel mode, jumps to a fixed handler address, the kernel validates the arguments, performs the work, and returns with the result — switching back to user mode on the way out.

System calls fall into familiar families. Process control: fork, exec, wait, exit. File management: open, read, write, close, lseek. Device management: ioctl, read/write on device files. Information maintenance: getpid, time. Communication: pipe, socket, send, recv, shared memory. Protection: chmod, chown. Parameters travel in registers (fastest, but limited in number), in a block of memory whose address is passed in a register (Linux uses registers for up to six arguments; larger structures go by pointer), or on the stack.

Crossing the boundary is not free. The CPU must switch modes, save and restore registers, possibly flush parts of the pipeline, and the kernel must check every pointer the user passed (never trust a pointer from user space). A system call costs on the order of a hundred nanoseconds to a microsecond — trivial once, painful a million times. That is why stdio buffers: fputc fills a user-space buffer and only calls write when it is full, turning thousands of calls into one. The worked example below puts numbers on that.
syscall.steps: Read a 1 MB file one byte at a time with read(fd, &ch, 1). How many system calls? Assume each call costs about 0.5 µs of crossing overhead alone. Now read it in 4 KB blocks. Overhead falls by a factor of 4096; the crossing cost becomes negligible.

interrupts.title: Interrupts, traps and exceptions
interrupts.body:
The CPU normally fetches and executes instructions in order. Three events can divert it. An interrupt is an asynchronous signal from outside the running instruction stream — a disk finished, a packet arrived, the timer expired, a key was pressed. A trap is a deliberate software-generated transfer, such as the system-call instruction. An exception (or fault) is raised by the instruction itself when something is wrong — divide by zero, illegal opcode, a page that is not in memory, an access outside the process’s limits. All three are handled the same way: the hardware saves the program counter and flags, looks up a handler address in the interrupt vector (an array indexed by the interrupt number) and jumps to it in kernel mode.

The handler — the interrupt service routine — does the minimum urgent work (acknowledge the device, copy a byte, wake a sleeping process) and returns. The kernel splits its work into a short top half that runs with interrupts disabled and a longer bottom half (softirq, tasklet, deferred work) that runs later with interrupts enabled, so the system stays responsive. Interrupts have priorities: a higher-priority interrupt may interrupt a lower-priority handler, but not the reverse, and the kernel can mask (temporarily ignore) interrupts in critical sections.

Compare the two ways of waiting for a device. With polling the CPU loops, reading a status register until it says “ready” — simple, and fast if the wait is a few cycles, but it burns the processor for the entire wait. With interrupt-driven I/O the CPU starts the operation, goes off to run another process, and is interrupted when the device finishes. For slow devices (a disk takes milliseconds, enough for millions of instructions) interrupts are enormously better. You will meet a third approach, DMA, in the I/O chapter.
interrupts.steps: A disk read takes 8 ms. The CPU runs at 3 × 10⁹ instructions/s (1 instruction per cycle for simplicity). How many instructions could it execute while it waits? Multiply.

structure.title: How kernels are organised
structure.body:
Everything above lives inside the kernel. How should that program itself be structured? There are five classic answers, and exam questions love to compare them. A monolithic kernel (traditional Unix, Linux) puts the scheduler, memory manager, file systems, network stack and drivers in one big program sharing one address space. Calls between parts are ordinary function calls, so it is fast; the price is that a bug in any driver can overwrite anything and crash the whole system. Linux softens this with loadable kernel modules: drivers and file systems that can be added to a running kernel without rebooting.

A layered design stacks strict levels — hardware at the bottom, user interface at the top — where each layer uses only the one below. It is easy to verify layer by layer (Dijkstra’s THE system was built this way), but layering is hard to apply cleanly (does the swap-space manager sit above or below the scheduler?) and each extra layer adds overhead. A microkernel (Mach, QNX, MINIX, L4, seL4) keeps in the privileged kernel only the bare minimum — address spaces, scheduling basics and inter-process communication — and runs file systems, drivers and the network stack as ordinary user-mode servers that exchange messages. A crashed driver is just a crashed process that can be restarted, which makes the system dependable and easy to extend; the cost is that every service call turns into messages and context switches.

Real systems are rarely pure. Hybrid kernels (Windows NT, macOS/XNU) keep a microkernel-like structure but run many services in kernel space for speed. Exokernels go to the other extreme: the kernel only multiplexes raw hardware securely and leaves all abstraction to application-linked library operating systems, giving applications maximum control. Finally, virtual machine structures run complete guest operating systems on top of a hypervisor — the subject of the last chapter.
structure.steps: A file read in a microkernel needs 2 messages (request and reply) between the application and the file server, and 2 more between the file server and the disk driver. If each message costs 3 µs and the monolithic version does the same work with plain calls costing 0.4 µs in total, what is the slowdown? Microkernel cost. Ratio to the monolithic cost.

boot.title: From power button to login prompt
boot.body:
At power-on there is no OS in memory, only firmware in non-volatile storage. The CPU starts executing at a fixed address and runs the firmware, which tests the hardware (POST), finds a boot device and loads a first program. Legacy BIOS reads the first 512-byte sector of the disk — the MBR — into memory and jumps to it. Those 512 bytes contain 446 bytes of boot code, a 64-byte partition table (four entries of 16 bytes) and a 2-byte signature (0x55AA). The code is far too small to load a kernel from a file system, so it merely loads a bigger bootloader (GRUB, LILO, the Windows Boot Manager) that does understand file systems.

Modern machines use UEFI: firmware that itself understands the FAT file system, reads a bootloader from an EFI system partition on a GPT disk, and can verify the bootloader’s digital signature (secure boot) so malware cannot slip in before the OS. Either way, the bootloader locates the kernel image, loads it into memory (together with an initial RAM disk containing the drivers needed to reach the real root file system), and jumps to it. The kernel then initialises memory management, the scheduler and devices, mounts the root file system, and starts the first user process — init or systemd on Linux — which in turn starts every service and finally the login prompt or the graphical shell.

The pattern to remember is bootstrapping: each stage is small and simple and is just capable enough to load the next, larger stage. That is why the sector is so tiny, why the bootloader is separate from the kernel, and why an OS can be updated by replacing files without touching the firmware.
boot.steps: Firmware reads sector 0 (512 bytes). How is it laid out? Boot code + partition table + signature. The partition table holds 4 entries; each entry is therefore how big?

history.title: How we got here: a short history of operating systems
history.body:
The features of a modern OS were each invented to cure a particular pain. The first computers had no OS: a programmer booked the machine, loaded a program by hand and watched it run. Setting up took longer than running, and the expensive CPU sat idle. Batch systems fixed the set-up cost: operators grouped similar jobs on cards or tape and a small resident monitor loaded them one after another. But a job waiting for the card reader or tape still left the CPU idle, because I/O devices were thousands of times slower than the processor.

The cure was multiprogramming: keep several jobs in memory at once, and when one waits for I/O let another use the CPU. This single idea creates almost everything in this course — memory management (several jobs must fit), CPU scheduling (which job next?), protection (jobs must not interfere), and synchronisation. Time-sharing extended it by switching so quickly (every few milliseconds) that many users at terminals each felt they had the machine to themselves; this brought interactive response, virtual memory and file systems with access control (CTSS, MULTICS, then UNIX). Personal computers returned to one user per machine but kept the ideas; distributed and cloud systems spread the same ideas over many machines; mobile and embedded systems added tight limits on power and memory; real-time systems added deadlines.

The derivation below turns the multiprogramming argument into a number — it is one of the most quoted results in the subject because it shows why an OS keeps several programs in memory.
history.steps: Suppose each process spends a fraction p of its time waiting for I/O (so it needs the CPU a fraction 1 − p of its time). With only one process in memory, the CPU is busy just 1 − p of the time. With n independent processes in memory, the CPU is idle only when all of them are waiting at the same moment. If the waits are independent, the probability they are all waiting is the product of their individual probabilities. The CPU is busy whenever at least one process is ready, which is the complement. The model is optimistic — it assumes independence and ignores context-switch overhead — but it explains the trend: more resident processes drive utilisation toward 100 %, with diminishing returns once p^n is small. The degree of multiprogramming n is limited by memory, which is why memory management matters. Each process waits for I/O 80 % of the time (p = 0.8). Utilisation with 4 processes in memory? 0.8⁴ = 0.4096. Adding a fifth process raises it to 1 − 0.8⁵ = 67.2 %, a gain of about 8 percentage points. Whether that extra process is worth its memory is a policy decision.

services.title: Services an operating system offers
services.body:
Pulling the threads together, a general-purpose OS offers a standard list of services, and examiners like asking for them. For the user and the programmer: a user interface (command line, graphical or touch); program execution (load a program, run it, end it normally or abnormally); I/O operations (programs may not touch devices directly, so the OS performs I/O on their behalf); file-system manipulation (create, delete, read, write, search, manage permissions); communication (processes on one machine or across a network exchange data, through shared memory or message passing); and error detection (hardware faults, device failures, bad programs).

For the system’s own sake the OS also provides resource allocation (CPU cycles, memory, files and devices to many users at once), accounting (who used what) and protection and security (controlling access to resources and defending against outsiders). These are not independent: protecting a file needs the file system; allocating memory needs the hardware’s protection registers; communication needs both. Notice also that the OS is itself a program that must be efficient — time spent running the OS is time not spent running your work, so every service has a cost that the designers constantly trade against its benefit.

summary.title: Summary and what comes next
summary.body:
• An OS is an extended machine (clean abstractions: file, process, address space, socket) and a resource manager (allocation, protection, accounting, sharing in time and space).
  • Hardware makes it possible: dual mode, privileged instructions, memory protection, a timer and interrupts.
  • User code enters the kernel only through system calls, interrupts and exceptions; each crossing has a cost, so libraries buffer.
  • Kernel designs trade speed against isolation: monolithic, layered, microkernel, hybrid, exokernel, virtual machine.
  • Booting is a chain of ever-larger loaders: firmware → bootloader → kernel → init.
  • Multiprogramming (utilisation = 1 − pⁿ) is the idea that created CPU scheduling, memory management and synchronisation.

Next, Chapter 2 opens the first abstraction: the process — what it is, how the OS represents it, and how the scheduler shares the CPU among many of them.
